title: Mixing modern and older players
summary: Cootie believed in blending modern players with older ones before Ellington did.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: -- you had a few problems with the band, because you had Joe Guy, you had Charlie, and you had Bud.
Well, that's what I meant when I said if they wasn't right, you know --
-- well, I could go along with them.
But when they were right, and played so wonderful.

Cootie, it's interesting, though. I mean, you were of a different generation. You were of the preceding generation for them. They were just starting in, coming up, kind of. Well, Charlie had more -- shared your background, to some extent, didn't he? Charlie Parker.
I mean, he started off coming out of that, didn't he?
But -- so -- but the whole thing was an integrated whole. Your style, their style, it all came together all right?
Yeah. Uh-huh. What I believed in was having modern jazz players and standard old players with the band.
Well, that's quite a tall order, blending them in together, isn't it?
Well, yeah. But it made sense to me.
Yeah. It was a challenge, too.
Well, in other words, you were breaking ground, too.
Well, in a way, but I think this was before Ellington thought of anything like this.
Because after -- the younger generation is the thing that keeps jazz alive.
And that's the reason why I had it.
